title: Check a meaning by swapping it in
statement: Have learners check a meaning they worked out from context by swapping it into the sentence: if the sentence no longer makes sense, the meaning is wrong.
example: One five-step procedure for working out a word's meaning ends on the swap-in check, done by the learner.
detail: The Grade 3 reading curriculum's procedure for working out a word or phrase, quoted in the reading course renderer, has five student-facing steps: spot the word, look inside it, look around it, try a meaning, then check by swapping the meaning into the sentence to see whether it still makes sense, a step the child does (`grade3-reading/course-renderer/docs/pedagogy/modelling-moment-procedures.md`, lines 417-423). Its correction route sends a learner back to the swap, and if the sentence doesn't make sense the meaning is wrong and they try again from the fourth step (lines 497-499). The curriculum's rulings kept all five steps because the swap-in check is real work (line 860). It is a design rule; nothing measured its effect.

evidence.quote: | 5 | Check by swapping in (CHILD) | "I swap my meaning into the sentence. Does the sentence still make sense?" |
Return to Step 5: "Swap your meaning in. Does the sentence still make sense?"
If it doesn't make sense, the meaning is wrong - try again from Step 4.
DECODE keeps its five steps (its Step 5, the swap-in check, is real work).
